title: What is the difference between an Entity (JPA-managed, maps to a table, never exposed), a DTO (plain class with validation, carries data across layers/API), and a POJO (framework-free plain object, may hold business logic), and when do you use each?
shortTitle: What is the difference between an Entity, a DTO, and a POJO, and when do you use each

s1_definition.profdef: An Entity is a JPA-managed class annotated with Entity that maps to a database table, is tracked by the persistence context, and should never be exposed directly through the API. A DTO is a plain class, often a record, that carries data across layers or the API boundary and typically holds validation annotations but no business logic. A POJO is any Plain Old Java Object, free of framework coupling, that may hold business logic and represent a domain concept. Entities are for persistence, DTOs are for transport, and POJOs are for framework-free domain modelling.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of three different documents at National Bank of India. The Entity is the official ledger record in the vault, managed under strict rules, tied to a specific row in the master book, and never handed to a customer. The DTO is the simple counter slip the clerk fills to pass information to or from the customer, with checkboxes to validate the form. The POJO is a scratch worksheet an analyst uses to calculate interest, following the bank's own rules, not tied to any system, just plain paper with logic written on it. Each document has a distinct purpose and you would not use one where another belongs.
s1_definition.oneliner: Entity persists to a table and stays internal, DTO transports data across boundaries with validation, POJO is a framework-free object that may carry domain logic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An Entity is a JPA-managed class annotated with Entity that maps to a database table, is tracked by the persistence context, and should never be exposed directly through the API. A DTO is a plain class, often a record, that carries data across layers or the API boundary and typically holds validation annotations but no business logic. A POJO is any Plain Old Java Object, free of framework coupling, that may hold business logic and represent a domain concept. Entities are for persistence, DTOs are for transport, and POJOs are for framework-free domain modelling.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of three different documents at National Bank of India. The Entity is the official ledger record in the vault, managed under strict rules, tied to a specific row in the master book, and never handed to a customer. The DTO is the simple counter slip the clerk fills to pass information to or from the customer, with checkboxes to validate the form. The POJO is a scratch worksheet an analyst uses to calculate interest, following the bank's own rules, not tied to any system, just plain paper with logic written on it. Each document has a distinct purpose and you would not use one where another belongs.

**One line to remember:** Entity persists to a table and stays internal, DTO transports data across boundaries with validation, POJO is a framework-free object that may carry domain logic.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's early code used one Account class for everything: it had JPA annotations, validation annotations, and was returned directly to clients. When the team lazy-loaded transactions, the serialiser hit the unloaded list outside the transaction and threw a LazyInitializationException, crashing the response. This is exactly why the entity should stay internal and a DTO should cross the boundary.

Problem 2 — The interest calculation logic was scattered and hard to test because it was mixed into the entity, which needed a database and persistence context to instantiate cleanly. This is exactly where a framework-free POJO value object helps. A Money POJO with an add and an applyInterest method can be unit tested with no database at all.

Problem 3 — Clients were sending requests that bound straight to the entity, and a malicious request once set a field it should not have. This is exactly why a request DTO with only the allowed fields, plus validation, is the right transport object.

We will build an account feature with a JPA-style entity for persistence, a request DTO and a response DTO for transport with validation, and a framework-free Money POJO that holds the interest logic. The demo shows the service receiving a DTO, using the entity internally, computing with the POJO, and returning a DTO, with the entity never exposed.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/layered-account-service-1.0.0.jar

# Open account: request DTO in, response DTO out (entity never exposed)
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","openingBalance":1000000.00}'
# {"accountId":"ACC-ab12cd","holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","balance":1000000.00}

# Apply 6% interest using the Money POJO logic
curl -s -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/ACC-ab12cd/interest?ratePercent=6"
# {"accountId":"ACC-ab12cd","holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","balance":1060000.00}
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a POST opening Rajesh's account with one million rupees, then a POST applying six percent interest.

Step 1: The open POST binds to an OpenAccountRequest, the request DTO. Validation checks the holder name is not blank and the opening balance is not negative. The DTO carries only the fields a client may send.

Step 2: The service receives the DTO and builds an Account entity with a generated id. The entity is saved through the repository and is JPA-managed, so it lives only inside the service and persistence layers.

Step 3: The service maps the entity to an AccountResponse, the response DTO, copying only the id, holder name, and balance. The entity never crosses the boundary, so there is no lazy-loading risk and no leaked field. The controller returns 201 with the DTO.

Step 4: The interest POST calls addYearlyInterest. The service wraps the entity balance in a Money POJO and calls applyInterest with six percent. The Money POJO, free of any framework, computes one million plus sixty thousand interest, scaled to two decimals, giving 1060000, and returns a new Money. This logic is pure and unit-testable without a database.

Step 5: The service sets the entity balance to the computed value. Because the entity is managed, that change would be flushed to the database. The service maps to a response DTO and returns it. The three object types each played their role: DTO on the wire, entity in persistence, POJO for logic.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 22:35:00 INFO  POST /accounts -> 201 {"accountId":"ACC-ab12cd","holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","balance":1000000.00}
2026-10-25 22:35:01 INFO  POST /accounts/ACC-ab12cd/interest?ratePercent=6
Money: 1000000.00 + interest 60000.00 = 1060000.00
2026-10-25 22:35:01 INFO  -> 200 {"accountId":"ACC-ab12cd","holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","balance":1060000.00}
(the Account ENTITY was never serialised to the client)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client: POST /accounts {holderName, openingBalance}
    │
    ▼
  OpenAccountRequest  ── DTO (validated, transport) ──
    │
    ▼
  AccountController → AccountService.open()
    │ build Account ENTITY (JPA-managed, internal)
    │ repo.save(entity)
    ▼
  toResponse(entity) → AccountResponse ── DTO out ──
    ▼
  201 {accountId, holderName, balance}   (ENTITY never leaves)

  ── Interest path (POJO logic) ─────────────────────
  POST /accounts/{id}/interest?ratePercent=6
    │
    ▼
  Money(entity.balance).applyInterest(6)  ── POJO, framework-free ──
    │ 1,000,000 + 60,000 = 1,060,000
    ▼
  entity.setBalance(1,060,000)  (managed → persisted)
    ▼
  AccountResponse DTO → 200
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Three Object Roles ═══

  ┌─ When to use each ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Entity: @Entity, maps table, JPA-managed → persistence │
  │          never exposed (leak/lazy-load/coupling risk)   │
  │  DTO:    plain/record, validation, no logic → transport │
  │          separate request vs response                   │
  │  POJO:   framework-free, may hold logic → domain/value  │
  │          pure, unit-testable without DB                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │ Account      │   │ OpenAccountReq   │   │ Money (POJO) │
  │ (ENTITY)     │   │ AccountResponse  │   │ applyInterest│
  │ @Id @Version │   │ (DTOs)           │   │ add/value    │
  └──────┬───────┘   └────────┬─────────┘   └──────┬───────┘
         │ persisted by        │ transported by      │ logic used by
         └──────────┬──────────┴──────────┬──────────┘
                    ▼                      ▼
             ┌───────────────────────────────┐
             │        AccountService         │
             │  open(req)→Response            │
             │  addYearlyInterest(id,rate)    │
             │  toResponse(entity)            │
             └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (interest) ───────────────────
  1. POST /accounts/{id}/interest?ratePercent=6
  2.   → service.addYearlyInterest
  3.     Money(balance).applyInterest(6) → 1,060,000 (POJO)
  4.     entity.setBalance(...)  (managed)
  5.   → toResponse → AccountResponse DTO
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An Entity, a DTO, and a POJO are three different kinds of object with three different jobs. An Entity is a JPA-managed class annotated with Entity that maps to a database table and is tracked by the persistence context, so it belongs to the persistence layer and should never be exposed directly. A DTO is a plain class, often a record, that carries data across layers or the API boundary, usually with validation annotations but no business logic. A POJO is any framework-free plain object that may hold business logic, like a value object representing money.

The reason the distinction matters is that each has risks if misused. In my work at National Bank of India, our early code used a single Account class with JPA annotations, validation annotations, and it was returned straight to clients. That caused a LazyInitializationException when the serialiser touched an unloaded transactions relationship outside a transaction, it leaked internal fields, and it coupled the API to the schema. Separating an internal entity from a response DTO fixed all three at once, because the entity stays below the service and only a safe DTO crosses the boundary.

The POJO earns its place in the domain logic. We had interest calculation mixed into the entity, which made it awkward to test because it dragged in persistence concerns. Moving that into a framework-free Money value object, with an applyInterest method using BigDecimal, let us unit test the logic with no database at all, and reuse it anywhere. So the entity persists, the DTO transports with validation, and the POJO holds pure logic.

When I decide which to use, I follow the layer. In the repository and persistence layer I use entities because that is what JPA manages. Across the API boundary and between layers I use DTOs because they are a stable, validated, decoupled contract, and I keep request and response DTOs separate so a client cannot mass-assign fields it should not. For framework-free domain rules and value objects I use POJOs so the logic stays pure and testable. Keeping the three roles separate, rather than collapsing them into one annotated entity, is exactly what makes a banking application well layered, secure, and easy to evolve.
